name: Wrist curl
angleNote: Wrist flexion: 0° = hand in line with the forearm, negative = bent back (stretched), positive = curled towards the palm. Elbow at the origin.

segments.massNote: Segment mass as a fraction of body mass, and centre of mass as a fraction of the segment length from its proximal end, from de Leva's adjusted Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov table (young adult males). The hand's centre of mass is given along wrist → third knuckle; here it is applied along wrist → grip, which is about as long.
segments.massSource: de Leva P (1996). Adjustments to Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov's segment inertia parameters. J Biomech 29(9):1223–1230. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(95)00178-6 (Table 4, males)
segments.note: Elbow→wrist and wrist→grip centre (bar in the fingers, about at the knuckles) in metres, typical adult. Estimates (TODO: anthropometric source).

strengthCurve.label: Wrist flexor strength
strengthCurve.note: Relative isometric wrist-flexion moment vs wrist angle (negative = bent back): strongest at 40° of flexion, about half that with the wrist bent back 60°. Average curve of 10 men, palm up (forearm supinated), elbow at 90°, fingers held flexed. Peak torque default 11 Nm: the average curve's peak (the men's individual peaks averaged 12.2 Nm, range 5–19).
strengthCurve.source: Delp SL, Grierson AE, Buchanan TS (1996). Maximum isometric moments generated by the wrist muscles in flexion-extension and radial-ulnar deviation. J Biomech 29(10):1371–1375. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(96)00029-2 (Fig. 2, read off; 10 men, forearm supinated, elbow at 90°)

weightsNote: Muscle weights (flexors): each muscle's moment-generating potential, PCSA × wrist moment arm, relative to the largest at that wrist angle; held flat outside the two angles given. If the load is shared to keep the summed squared activation smallest, activation scales with this potential, so the bars show that pattern, not EMG. The finger flexors are included because they cross the wrist: Gonzalez et al. found they supply about 68% of the flexion potential at 40° of flexion (the long finger and wrist extensors about 45% and 55% of the extension potential).
weightsSource: Gonzalez RV, Buchanan TS, Delp SL (1997). How muscle architecture and moment arms affect wrist flexion-extension moments. J Biomech 30(7):705–712. doi:10.1016/S0021-9290(97)00015-8 (Table 1: PCSA × moment arm at neutral, at 40° of flexion for the flexors and 20° of extension for the extensors)

muscles.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
muscles.note: Strongest pure wrist flexor, on the little-finger side; still only about half the finger flexors' potential.

muscles.name: Flexor carpi radialis
muscles.note: Wrist flexor on the thumb side.

muscles.name: Palmaris longus
muscles.note: Small wrist flexor; absent in some people.

muscles.name: Flexor digitorum superficialis
muscles.note: Finger flexor that also crosses the wrist, with a large cross-section and moment arm: one of the two main movers of a wrist curl.

muscles.name: Flexor digitorum profundus
muscles.note: Deep finger flexor; the only one that bends the fingertips. Its wrist potential is the largest of all wrist flexors, so it leads in a wrist curl.

phases.name: Bottom
phases.text: Wrist bent back, flexors stretched and at their weakest (less than half their best). Seated, the torque is still near its peak, so the sticking point lies here, around 30° bent back; behind the back the load barely pulls against the flexors here.

phases.name: Middle
phases.text: Hand in line with the forearm. Seated with the forearm flat, the weight is furthest from the wrist horizontally (largest torque), but the flexors are stronger here than bent back.

phases.name: Top
phases.text: Wrist curled. Seated, the weight moves back over the wrist and gets easier; behind the back the moment arm keeps growing to the top.

variants.name: Seated wrist curl (dumbbell, palm up)
variants.notes: Forearm flat on the thigh, palm up, hand over the knee. Gravity pulls straight down, so the moment arm is the hand's horizontal reach: torque ∝ cos(wrist angle), largest with the hand level (0°) and smaller both in the stretched bottom and at the top.

variants.name: Behind-the-back barbell wrist curl
variants.notes: Standing, arms hanging, bar behind the thighs, palms facing back. The forearm is vertical, so torque ∝ sin(wrist angle): nothing with the hand hanging straight, most at full flexion — the opposite of the seated version. Load per hand (half the bar). Bending back (negative angles) is blocked by the legs here; the load would help, not resist.

variants.name: Cable wrist curl (low pulley)
variants.notes: Forearm on the thigh or a bench, cable from a low pulley in front of the hand. The cable pulls towards the pulley instead of straight down, so the top of the curl keeps more tension than with a dumbbell. Move the pulley to see the peak shift.

variants.name: Seated barbell wrist curl with finger roll
variants.notes: Same wrist torque as the dumbbell version (per hand). At the bottom the bar rolls down to the fingertips and the fingers curl it back up before the wrist flexes. The finger joints aren't modelled here, so the extra finger work only shows as a higher estimated share for the two finger flexors (estimate, TODO).
